Name: Massalia, Hub of the Gallic Alliance: The Greek Colonial Emporium at the Mouth of the Rhone
RagShortTexts: Massalia is an independent merchant oligarchy founded by Phocaean Greeks in southern Gaul
It guards the shipping corridor at the mouth of the Rhone and is Rome's oldest and most loyal maritime ally
It gave the army of the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio forward intelligence in Gaul and watched Hannibal's river crossing
BaseText: Massalia (town_rome_massalia, modern Marseille) was founded around 600 BC by Greek refugees from Phocaea in Asia Minor, and it is the most famous Greek city-state of learning, shipbuilding and trade in the western Mediterranean. The city is built around a fine natural bay embraced on three sides by steep headlands, and it guards the inland Gallic river and land trade routes at the mouth of the Rhone, monopolizing the onward shipment of Gallic tin, amber and wine. As a close friend bound to Rome by a blood alliance from Rome's earliest days, Massalia's oligarchic council of six hundred firmly pursued a pro-Roman course. In 218 BC, when Hannibal led his army over the Pyrenees, it was Massalia's patrolling light cavalry and scouts who first brought the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio the secret intelligence that Hannibal was forcing a crossing of the Rhone, and throughout the war the city remained Rome's steadfast eyes and ears and naval base in the west.

Variants.Content: We lit the light of Athena's wisdom on this wild Gallic headland. Our alliance with Rome has kept us standing for centuries, and every merchant ship at the mouth of the Rhone guards our independence.

Massalia is Rome's most loyal friend in foreign lands. Without the warnings of Massalia's sailors and scouts, General Publius Cornelius Scipio could never have seen through the barbarian Hannibal's river-crossing ruse.

The Greek merchants build high walls on the bay to count their gold, and they have brought the Roman robbers into the hunting grounds of the Gauls. One day the Celtic war axe will split their ivory abacus.
